findings.message: apps/web/src/devLatency.ts DelayLine.push keeps order only on paper. It clamps each item's due time to the previous item's (`at = max(last, now + delay)`), then schedules every item with its own `setTimeout(deliver, at - now)`. Two clamped items share the same `at`, but real timers do not fire them in push order. In Node, the timer expiry is libuv-now (whole ms, cached per loop turn) plus the fractional delay. So when two messages are pushed in the same loop turn (for example two WebSocket frames from one read) and the second is clamped, the second gets the strictly earlier expiry and fires first. In the browser, WebIDL truncates the delay to whole ms, so a clamped item fires first whenever its fractional offset is smaller, which is about half of clamped pairs spaced more than 1 ms apart. The unit tests use vitest fake timers, which order by exact time and then insertion, so they cannot see this. The acceptance clause that the dev latency tests fail when ordering breaks therefore holds only under fake timers. At ?rtt=80&jitter=20 the effect is mostly harmless reordering between different message kinds (a bundle against a patch or probe). With larger jitter, or after a main-thread stall that batches arrivals, it reorders frame bundles, which the rollback treats as a gap and waits for a snapshot to fix, and it can reorder Colyseus state patches. That distorts the operator's playtest, the one thing this setting exists for. Fix: use one FIFO queue per direction drained by a single timer, as packages/test-tools/src/impairmentProxy.ts Pipe already does.
findings.requirement: delay outgoing and incoming messages, probes included, by about RTT/2 each way, add bounded jitter, and never reorder

findings.message: apps/web/src/duel.test.ts:284-321 ('delays the room's socket both ways...') tests only the base delay for the outgoing path of applyDevLatency. The shared draw list [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.999999, 0] gives both outgoing messages (the probe echo and the input) a draw of 0.5, which means zero jitter, and they are sent 40 ms apart, so they could never reorder. Only the incoming bundles use extreme draws. The DelayLine unit tests (lines 211-263) do cover the jitter bound and ordering, but a regression in the wrapper's send side would pass every test: a DelayLine per send, a plain setTimeout, or an outgoing line built without jitter. The integration test would not catch it either, because redundant inputs mask stale-sequence drops. Suggested fix: send two outgoing messages a few ms apart with draws 0.999999 then 0, and assert that they leave in order at the jitter bounds.
findings.requirement: delay outgoing and incoming messages, probes included, by about RTT/2 each way, add bounded jitter, and never reorder
